summary: Describes the Multicast Transport Protocol, a reliable transport that uses the multicast ability of the networks underneath it. It lets a group of receivers get the same data reliably from a sender. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Instead of mailing the same letter to each friend, you send it once and many friends get it. This protocol also makes sure everyone really got every page.

subtitle: A transport protocol for reliable multicast messaging between groups of processes.

tldr.problem: Applications that need to send data reliably to multiple recipients usually must send the same data many times, once to each destination. Multicasting at the network layer does not guarantee reliability.
tldr.mechanism: MTP adds reliable delivery on top of multicast or broadcast capability, using a master process to coordinate transmit tokens, sequence numbers and message acceptance acknowledgments.
tldr.outcome: A group of processes can collaborate with atomic multicast delivery: all members agree on message order and receipt status even if the network partitions.

today: RFC 1301 is an Informational RFC describing an experimental transport protocol for reliable multicast. It has not been standardized as an Internet Standard and is primarily of historical interest. The multicast transport problem has since been addressed by other protocols.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem
sections.content:
The Multicast Transport Protocol (MTP) is a transport layer protocol designed to deliver data reliably to a group of processes using multicast or broadcast network capability. Unlike TCP which provides reliable point-to-point connections, MTP enables a collection of processes (called a web) to receive the same data reliably without requiring the sender to transmit multiple copies.

MTP adds flow control, sequencing and agreement mechanisms on top of the underlying network's multicast capability. The protocol is atomic: all members agree on the order and acceptance status of every message, even if the network partitions temporarily.
sections.eli5: MTP is like a radio station that broadcasts to many listeners, but with extra rules to make sure everyone hears the same show in the same order and nobody gets confused if someone's radio cuts out.

sections.title: Architecture and Roles
sections.content:
An MTP web consists of a master process and one or more member processes. The master instantiates and controls the web, managing membership and performance. Members have roles: a consumer receives data only, a producer may transmit data, and the master is the principal process with all privileges.

MTP uses three fundamental parameters: heartbeat (time interval in milliseconds between packets), window (maximum data packets per heartbeat), and retention (how many heartbeat periods to buffer data for retransmission). These parameters control quality of service and are negotiated when members join.
sections.eli5: There is one leader (the master) and everyone else listens and sometimes talks. The leader sends a steady pulse (heartbeat) to keep everyone synchronized, decides who gets to talk when (window), and remembers old messages long enough to resend them if someone missed them (retention).

sections.title: Packet Format and Fields
sections.content:
Every MTP packet starts with a fixed transport header followed by variable data. The header contains: protocol version, packet type and modifier, a client subchannel field, source and destination connection identifiers, message acceptance criteria, heartbeat, window and retention values.

Packet types include data (for user information), nak (negative acknowledgment requests), empty (for synchronization when no data is available), join (to add members), quit (to leave), token (to request or grant transmit rights), and isMember (to verify membership).
sections.eli5: Every packet has a label saying what kind of message it is (data, please-resend, join the group, leave the group, etc.) and information about timing and flow control.

sections.title: Operation and Data Flow
sections.content:
Before transmitting user data, a producer must request and receive a transmit token from the master. The master grants tokens in order, assigning each a message sequence number. The producer then multicasts data packets in bursts (windows) separated by heartbeat intervals. The producer may retransmit any packet within the retention window if a consumer sends a nak[request].

Consumers receive all multicast data and use packet sequence numbers to detect loss. If packets are missing, they send a nak[request] to the producer, who multicasts the requested packets again. The master tracks message status as accepted, pending or rejected, communicating this in every packet so all members agree on which messages are reliable.
sections.eli5: To send a message, you ask the master for permission (the token). While you have it, you send your data in chunks. If someone missed a chunk, they ask you to send it again. The master keeps score of whose message actually made it.

sections.title: Joining and Leaving
sections.content:
A new process joins by sending a join[request] to the web's unknown TSAP (transport service access point), specifying its desired role and quality of service requirements. The master responds with join[confirm] or join[deny]. Once confirmed, the new member learns the web's multicast address and current parameters from the join[confirm] message.

Members leave voluntarily by sending quit[request] to the master, or may be banished if they violate the protocol. The master can also terminate the entire web by multicasting a quit[request] to all members.
sections.eli5: To join the group, you knock on the door and say what you want to do. The master either welcomes you and tells you where to listen, or says no thanks. To leave, you say goodbye.

sections.title: Reliability Mechanisms and Parameters
sections.content:
MTP provides reliability through several mechanisms. The message acceptance record tracks the status of the last 12 messages, allowing all members to agree on delivery. The retention parameter determines how long producers buffer data for potential retransmission; typical values are 3 to 5 heartbeats. NAK-based recovery allows consumers to request only the data they missed, reducing unnecessary retransmission.

The protocol is designed for networks with low corruption rates. Recommended heartbeat values are 160-200 milliseconds for local area networks, with window sizes of 17-20 packets per heartbeat, yielding approximately 180 kilobytes per second throughput. For multi-network webs, larger retention values suppress duplicate NAK requests from different networks.
sections.eli5: Everyone remembers which messages definitely got through and which might be lost. If you miss something, you ask for just that part, and the sender keeps old messages around long enough to send them again if you ask.

fields.name: Packet Type
fields.desc: Type of packet: data, nak, empty, join, quit, token, or isMember.

fields.name: Packet Type Modifier
fields.desc: Variant of the packet type, such as eow (end of window) or eom (end of message) for data packets.

fields.name: Client Subchannel
fields.desc: Semantics defined by the transport client.

fields.name: Source Connection ID
fields.desc: Unique identifier of the sending transport instance.

fields.name: Destination Connection ID
fields.desc: Target web's connection identifier or unknown (0x00000000) for join.

fields.name: Message Acceptance
fields.desc: Status of the last 12 messages and synchronization flag.

fields.name: Heartbeat
fields.desc: Timing interval in milliseconds, shared by all web members.

fields.name: Window
fields.desc: Maximum data packets allowed per heartbeat.

fields.name: Retention
fields.desc: Number of heartbeat intervals to retain data for retransmission.
